1.1: [To To Lycurgus of Sparta] You have come to my rich temple, Lycurgus, a man dear to Zeus and to all who have Olympian homes. I am in doubt whether to pronounce you man or god, but I think rather you are a god, Lycurgus.

2.1: [To To Lycurgus on wealth] Love of money and nothing else will ruin Sparta.

3.1: [To To the Therans on Libya (third oracle)] Know you better than I, fair Libya abounding in fleeces? Better the stranger than he who has trod it? Oh! Clever Therans!

4.1: [To To Solon on Salamis] First sacrifice to the warriors who once had their home in this island, whom now the rolling plain of fair Asopia covers, laid in the tombs of heroes with their faces turned to the sunset.

5.1: [To To Solon on his reforms] Seat yourself now amidships, for you are the pilot of Athens. Grasp the helm fast in your hands; you have many allies in your city.

6.1: [To To Croesus on his identity (the tortoise oracle)] I know the number of the sand and the measure of the sea; I understand the speech of the dumb and hear the voiceless. The smell has come to my sense of a hard-shelled tortoise being cooked with a lamb's flesh in a bronze pot: bronze is the cauldron underneath, and bronze is the lid.

7.1: [To To Croesus on his monarchy] Whenever a mule shall become sovereign king of the Medians, then, Lydian Delicate-Foot, flee by the stone-strewn Hermus, flee, and think not to stand fast, nor shame to be chicken-hearted.

8.1: [To To the Spartans on Arcadia] You ask me for Arcadia? You ask too much; I grant it not. There are many men in Arcadia, eaters of acorns, who will hinder you. But I grudge you not. I will give you Tegea to beat with your feet in dancing, and its fair plain to measure with a rope.

9.1: [To To the Siphnians] When the Prytanies' seat shines white in the island of Siphnos, white-browed all the forum — need then of a true seer's wisdom — danger will threat from a wooden boat, and a herald in scarlet.

10.1: [To To Athens on Xerxes (first oracle)] Now your statues are standing and pouring sweat. They shiver with dread. The black blood drips from the highest rooftops. They have seen the necessity of evil. Get out, get out of my sanctum and drown your spirits in woe.

11.1: [To To Athens on Xerxes (second oracle — the wooden wall)] Await not in quiet the coming of the horses, the marching feet, the armed host upon the land. Slip away. Turn your back. You will meet in battle anyway. O holy Salamis, you will be the death of many a woman's son between the seedtime and the harvest of the grain.

12.1: [To To Sparta on Xerxes] Hear your fate, O dwellers in Sparta of the wide spaces; either your famed, great town must be sacked by Perseus' sons, or, if that be not, the whole land of Lacedaemon shall mourn the death of a king of the house of Heracles, for not the strength of lions or of bulls shall hold him, strength against strength; for he has the power of Zeus, and will not be checked until one of these two he has consumed.

13.1: [To To the Delphians on the Persians] Pray to the Winds. They will prove to be mighty allies of Greece.

14.1: [To To Chaerephon on Socrates] Sophocles is wise, Euripides is wiser, but of all men Socrates is wisest.

15.1: [To To Sparta on Lysander] Also the dragon, earthborn, in craftiness coming behind thee.

16.1: [To To Sparta on the lame king] Sure though thy feet, proud Sparta, have a care, a lame king's reign may see thee trip — Beware! Troubles unlooked for long shall vex thy shore, and rolling Time his tide of carnage pour.

17.1: [To To Philip II of Macedon] With silver spears you may conquer the world.

18.1: [To To Alexander the Great] You are invincible, my son.

19.1: [To To Zeno of Citium] Become of the same complexion as the dead — apply yourself to the reading of the books of the ancients.

20.1: [To To the Delphians on the Celtic invasion] Care for these things fall on me!

21.1: [To To Cicero on fame] Make your own nature, not the advice of others, your guide in life.

22.1: [To To Julian the Apostate (the last oracle)] Tell the king: the ornate hall has fallen to the ground. Apollo no longer has his shelter, his laurel grove, nor his prophetic spring; the speaking water has run dry.
